Rust has no exceptions. Errors are values, returned as Result<T, E>. This is the single biggest structural difference from Python/Java/JS, and it is worth learning properly because half of all Rust code review comments are about it.

The two kinds of failure

Recoverable Unrecoverable
Example file not found, invalid input, network timeout index out of bounds, assertion failure, bug
Mechanism Result<T, E> panic!
Caller's job handle it nothing — the process aborts or unwinds

Rule of thumb: panic! is for programmer errors (invariant violations). Result is for expected failures. "The user typed garbage" is not a panic; "this match arm is unreachable but I got here anyway" is.

panic!

Things that panic implicitly:

Unwinding vs aborting

By default a panic unwinds: it runs destructors up the stack and then the thread ends. That is safe but costs binary size.

Use abort for binaries where you never catch panics (most servers and CLIs). Keep unwinding if you use catch_unwind (e.g. a web framework isolating a handler's panic).

unwrap, expect, ?

Rule of thumb: unwrap() is acceptable in tests, examples, and where the compiler has already proven the value exists (split_once right after a contains check). Everywhere else, use ? or expect with a message that explains what was being attempted.

The From::from is why ? can convert error types automatically: if impl From<io::Error> for MyError exists, ? in a function returning Result<_, MyError> just works.

Defining your own error type, by hand

source() builds an error chain, which anyhow and most loggers print as "caused by: ...". This is what makes a stack trace of causes possible without a backtrace.

thiserror — the derive version

In practice nobody writes the above by hand.

One attribute does the Display, the Error, and the From. Use thiserror for library error types — the enum is public API, callers can match on variants, and the type has no hidden dependencies.

#[source] and #[from]

anyhow — the application version

anyhow::Error is a boxed dyn Error with a context chain. It is for binaries: you print it, you do not match on it.

With {:#} formatting you get the whole chain on one line; {:?} gives the multi-line version with a backtrace if RUST_BACKTRACE=1.

The rule

Crate type Error type
Library (others call it) thiserror enum — typed, matchable, #[non_exhaustive]
Application / binary anyhow::Result<T> — context, no ceremony
Both thiserror in the domain crate, anyhow at the edges

Gotcha: never expose anyhow::Error in a public library API. Callers cannot match on it, cannot retry intelligently, and it locks them to your crate's version of anyhow.

Converting between them

Error handling in main

Three shapes, in increasing order of usefulness:

Shape 2 is the one to reach for in a CLI. Shape 3 when the exit code matters (e.g. 2 for usage errors, like grep).

Retries and backoff

Retry only transient errors: timeouts, 5xx, connection resets. Retrying a 400 or a validation error just wastes time. This is why typed errors matter — anyhow cannot tell you which kind you got.

Error design principles

1. Make the error message actionable. Include the value, the key, the path.

2. Do not lose the source. Always wire #[source]/#[from] so the chain survives. format!("{e}") into a new String error throws away the cause.

3. Mark public error enums #[non_exhaustive].

This lets you add variants without a breaking change, because callers cannot exhaustively match.

4. Return Result from constructors that validate. A smart constructor is the only way to guarantee a type's invariant.

5. Do not return Result when nothing can fail. fn name(&self) -> &str, not -> Result<&str, Infallible>.

Exercises

  1. Write fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> with a thiserror enum covering "empty", "not a number" and "out of range".
  2. Add #[from] std::io::Error and confirm ? works without a manual From.
  3. Convert a thiserror enum into anyhow::Result at a binary boundary with .context("loading config") and print the chain with {:#}.
  4. Write a retry helper that only retries a Transient variant of your own error enum, and immediately returns on Permanent.
  5. Find every unwrap() in a small project and classify each as (a) provably safe, (b) should be ?, (c) should be expect with a message.
